title: Musculoskeletal Nutritional Deficiencies: Osteomalacia, Rickets, and Scurvy
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the three classic nutritional diseases of the skeleton. Osteomalacia and rickets are one defect, failed mineralization of osteoid, seen after and before growth plate closure. Scurvy is the opposite kind of defect: mineral handling is normal, but the collagen matrix itself is unstable because vitamin C is missing. Board questions usually give a lab panel, a radiograph description, or a child with bowed legs or painful limbs and ask you to name the defect, the missing step, and the reason each finding appears. If you can explain why phosphate, not calcium, usually limits mineralization, and why unhydroxylated collagen falls apart at body temperature, the findings follow.

connections.how: The activation pathway and the PTH and FGF23 loops taught there explain every laboratory value in vitamin D deficiency and X-linked hypophosphatemia.
Scurvy is a defect at the intracellular hydroxylation step of collagen synthesis, the pathway in which osteogenesis imperfecta and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome arise at other steps.
Celiac disease, cystic fibrosis, cholestasis, and bariatric surgery reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamin D through loss of micelles and chylomicrons.

connections.to: Renal physiology and chronic kidney disease
connections.how: The proximal tubule makes calcitriol and reabsorbs phosphate, so tubular disease and loss of renal mass cause mineralization defects.
Scurvy bleeds from fragile vessels with normal platelets and coagulation tests, and it impairs nonheme iron absorption.

Defective mineralization of newly formed osteoid at remodeling sites in the adult skeleton, producing soft bone with wide osteoid seams.
Defective mineralization of the growing skeleton, affecting both the growth plate cartilage and newly formed osteoid, before the plates close.

The main circulating vitamin D metabolite made in the liver, whose serum level reflects body vitamin D stores.

Fibroblast growth factor 23, an osteocyte hormone that causes phosphaturia and lowers calcitriol production.
A pseudofracture: a narrow lucent band running across part of the cortex, filled with unmineralized osteoid, typical of osteomalacia.
An iron-containing enzyme of the endoplasmic reticulum that converts proline in procollagen to hydroxyproline and needs ascorbate to keep its iron reduced.
Small hemorrhages around hair follicles, mainly on the legs, caused by fragile capillaries in scurvy.
Bleeding beneath the periosteum, which lifts it from the bone; a painful feature of scurvy in children.

sections.title: How vitamin D deficiency and phosphate loss stop osteoid from mineralizing

blocks.text: Bone forms in two steps. Osteoblasts first secrete osteoid, a collagen-rich matrix, and mineral is then deposited in it as hydroxyapatite over the following days to weeks. Mineralization needs an adequate product of calcium and phosphate in the extracellular fluid, matrix vesicles from osteoblasts, and tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, which destroys pyrophosphate, a natural inhibitor of crystal growth. When the calcium phosphate product is too low, osteoblasts keep making osteoid but it stays soft.

Vitamin D deficiency lowers that product mainly through phosphate. Without calcitriol, the gut absorbs less calcium and phosphate. The small fall in ionized calcium raises PTH, which restores calcium by increasing bone resorption, distal tubular calcium reabsorption, and 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity. PTH also removes phosphate transporters from the proximal tubule, so phosphate is lost in the urine. The result is a near-normal calcium and a low phosphate, and the low phosphate is what fails mineralization. Primary phosphate loss through the kidney, as with excess FGF23 or proximal tubular injury, reaches the same end without vitamin D deficiency.

blocks.title: From vitamin D deficiency to unmineralized osteoid
steps: Low 25-hydroxyvitamin D limits calcitriol
Gut absorbs less calcium and phosphate
Ionized calcium falls slightly; PTH rises
PTH restores calcium from bone and kidney
PTH causes phosphaturia; serum phosphate falls
Calcium phosphate product too low to mineralize
Osteoid accumulates in wide unmineralized seams
blocks.caption: Secondary hyperparathyroidism protects serum calcium at the cost of phosphate, which is why phosphate is usually the limiting ion.

blocks.text: The skeletal result depends on whether growth plates are open. In a child, the defect involves both the growth plate and new bone. Without enough phosphate, hypertrophic chondrocytes fail to undergo apoptosis, the cartilage is not mineralized or invaded by vessels, and the plate becomes thick and disorganized (MS-2); the metaphyseal bone formed beneath it is also poorly mineralized. This is rickets. After the plates close, only remodeling sites are affected: each osteon or trabecular packet refilled by osteoblasts stays partly unmineralized. This is osteomalacia. The amount of matrix is normal or increased, but the matrix is soft, so bones bend and develop insufficiency fractures.

blocks.title: Causes of defective mineralization grouped by mechanism
rows: Low sun exposure, low intake, fat malabsorption
Severe liver disease; CKD; inherited 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) or vitamin D receptor defects
Receptor defects give high calcitriol, often with alopecia
X-linked hypophosphatemia, tumor-induced osteomalacia (FGF23), Fanconi syndrome
Very low dietary calcium in some regions
Low alkaline phosphatase, the reverse of other causes
blocks.caption: Every cause either lowers the calcium phosphate product at bone or leaves pyrophosphate uncleared.

blocks.predict: A patient with severe vitamin D deficiency has a normal serum calcium. Why can bone still fail to mineralize?
blocks.explain: Secondary hyperparathyroidism keeps calcium normal by drawing on bone and kidney, but PTH also causes phosphaturia. Serum phosphate falls, so the calcium phosphate product at the osteoid is too low even though calcium looks normal.

sections.title: Risk factors for vitamin D deficiency and the step each one blocks

blocks.text: Each risk factor acts at one point in the supply and activation pathway (MS-8): skin synthesis, intake and absorption, hepatic 25-hydroxylation, renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation, or catabolism. Placing a risk factor on that pathway predicts what the laboratory panel will show.

Skin synthesis supplies most vitamin D for many people, so anything that reduces ultraviolet B (UVB) reaching the epidermis matters. High latitude in winter, indoor living, covering clothing, sunscreen, and older age (less 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin) all reduce production. Melanin absorbs UVB, so darker skin needs considerably longer exposure to make the same amount, and people with darker skin living at high latitude carry a high risk.

Infants depend on stores transferred across the placenta and then on diet. Human milk contains little vitamin D, so an exclusively breastfed infant who is not supplemented and has little sun exposure, especially one born to a vitamin D deficient mother, is the classic rickets case. The risk is greatest in infants with darker skin.

Vitamin D is fat soluble. It is absorbed in bile acid micelles and leaves the enterocyte in chylomicrons, so any cause of fat malabsorption, such as cholestasis, pancreatic insufficiency, celiac disease, Crohn disease of the ileum, or bariatric surgery, causes deficiency. Liver disease reduces 25-hydroxylation only when severe, and cholestatic disease acts mainly by reducing bile flow and absorption. Kidney disease reduces calcitriol by loss of proximal tubule mass, and nephrotic syndrome adds urinary loss of 25-hydroxyvitamin D bound to its binding protein.

Some anticonvulsants, notably phenytoin, phenobarbital, and carbamazepine, induce hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, chiefly CYP3A4, through the pregnane X receptor. These enzymes convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D and calcitriol to inactive polar metabolites, so stores fall despite normal intake. Rifampin acts the same way, and glucocorticoids oppose calcitriol action on intestinal calcium absorption. Obesity lowers serum levels because the vitamin is sequestered in adipose tissue.

sections.title: Osteomalacia: bone pain, proximal weakness, Looser zones, and the laboratory pattern

blocks.text: Osteomalacia develops slowly and is often mistaken for osteoporosis or a muscle disease. The findings follow from soft, unmineralized bone and from low phosphate.

Bone pain is diffuse and aching, worst in the lower back, pelvis, hips, and legs, with tenderness when the sternum, ribs, or tibiae are pressed. The pain is thought to come from unmineralized osteoid that hydrates and expands beneath the richly innervated periosteum. Proximal muscle weakness, often with a waddling gait and difficulty rising from a chair, is partly explained by low phosphate, which limits ATP and creatine phosphate in muscle, and partly by loss of calcitriol action on vitamin D receptors in muscle fibers. Muscle enzymes are usually normal, which helps separate it from an inflammatory myopathy.

Looser zones (pseudofractures) are the characteristic radiographic sign. They are narrow lucent bands, often bilateral and symmetric, running perpendicular to the cortex and partway across the bone, typically in the medial femoral neck, pubic rami, ribs, lateral border of the scapula, and proximal ulna. They are insufficiency fractures that have healed with unmineralized osteoid instead of bone. Bone density is low on densitometry, which cannot distinguish osteomalacia from osteoporosis. Bone biopsy after double tetracycline labeling shows wide osteoid seams and a prolonged mineralization lag time.

The laboratory pattern in vitamin D deficiency follows directly from C01. 25-hydroxyvitamin D is low, often below about 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L). PTH is high. Calcium is low or low normal because PTH defends it, and urine calcium is low. Phosphate is low from phosphaturia and poor absorption. Alkaline phosphatase is high because osteoblasts are active, laying down osteoid that does not mineralize. Calcitriol is often normal or even high, since PTH drives 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which is why it is not a test of vitamin D status.

blocks.title: Laboratory patterns in adult bone disease
blocks.caption: Osteoporosis is less bone of normal composition, so its labs are normal; osteomalacia is matrix that has not mineralized. Reference ranges vary by laboratory.

blocks.title: Reading an osteomalacia panel
blocks.text: A 70-year-old woman who rarely goes outdoors has hip pain and trouble climbing stairs. Calcium is 8.6 mg/dL, phosphate 2.0 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 240 U/L, PTH 140 pg/mL, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 7 ng/mL. Start with the low 25-hydroxyvitamin D: stores are depleted. The high PTH explains why calcium is low normal rather than low, and the PTH-driven phosphaturia explains the low phosphate. The high alkaline phosphatase shows active osteoblasts making osteoid that cannot mineralize. Osteoporosis alone would give normal values throughout, and primary hyperparathyroidism would give a high, not low normal, calcium.

sections.title: Rickets: skeletal signs, radiographs, and X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets

blocks.text: Rickets appears where bone grows fastest, so the signs depend on age. In the first year the skull and ribs grow rapidly; once the child walks, the weight-bearing long bones take the strain. Each sign is either an expanded growth plate, accumulated soft osteoid, or soft bone bending under load.

blocks.title: Rickets findings and their mechanisms
rows: Skull bones dent inward under pressure and spring back
Thin, poorly mineralized membranous bone; usually in infants under about 6 months
Square, prominent forehead; delayed fontanelle closure
Excess unmineralized osteoid on the skull vault
Smooth, rounded knobs along the costochondral junctions
Thickened, unmineralized growth cartilage at the rib ends
Horizontal groove along the lower ribs
Diaphragm pulls inward on soft ribs
Soft long bones bend under body weight
Delayed tooth eruption, enamel defects, short stature
Poor mineralization of teeth and slow linear growth
Widened physis; frayed, cupped, splayed metaphyses
Disorganized cartilage and unmineralized osteoid at the metaphysis
blocks.caption: The radiographic changes are clearest at the distal radius and ulna and around the knee, where growth is fastest.

blocks.text: Some bowing is normal: toddlers have physiologic genu varum until about 18 to 24 months, followed by physiologic valgus. Bowing that persists, worsens, or comes with metaphyseal changes points to rickets. Nutritional rickets also brings the consequences of low calcium and low phosphate: hypotonia, delayed walking, a protuberant abdomen, and, when calcium finally falls, tetany or seizures, especially in young infants.
X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets

X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH) is the most common inherited form of rickets. Loss-of-function mutations in PHEX, an endopeptidase expressed in osteoblasts and osteocytes, raise FGF23 production by a mechanism not fully defined. FGF23 acts on the proximal tubule through FGF receptor 1 and its coreceptor alpha-Klotho. It removes the sodium phosphate cotransporters NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc, causing phosphaturia, and it suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase while inducing 24-hydroxylase, so calcitriol is low or inappropriately normal despite low phosphate. The gut therefore cannot compensate.

blocks.title: How PHEX loss causes hypophosphatemic rickets
steps: PHEX loss of function in osteocytes
FGF23 production rises
Proximal tubule loses NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc
Phosphaturia; serum phosphate falls
Calcitriol stays low or inappropriately normal
Gut phosphate absorption does not increase
Rickets or osteomalacia without hypocalcemia
blocks.caption: Calcium is normal because the primary defect is phosphate wasting, not loss of vitamin D.

blocks.text: Because calcium stays normal and PTH is normal or only mildly raised, XLH lacks tetany and has little myopathy. The leg bowing, disproportionate short stature, and spontaneous dental abscesses (from defective dentin) dominate, and adults develop painful enthesopathy and osteomalacia. Inheritance is X-linked dominant: an affected father passes it to all daughters and no sons. Autosomal dominant hypophosphatemic rickets, from FGF23 mutations that resist cleavage, and tumor-induced osteomalacia produce the same biochemistry.

blocks.title: Nutritional rickets versus X-linked hypophosphatemia
blocks.caption: Normal calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D with low phosphate point to a phosphate-wasting disorder.

blocks.predict: Why does a child with XLH not develop tetany, although the bones are as soft as in nutritional rickets?
blocks.explain: Tetany comes from low ionized calcium. In XLH the defect is renal phosphate loss driven by FGF23, so calcium absorption and PTH regulation of calcium are intact and calcium stays normal. Mineralization fails only because phosphate is low.

sections.title: How vitamin C deficiency produces unstable collagen

blocks.text: Humans cannot make ascorbate because the gene for L-gulonolactone oxidase, the last enzyme of the synthetic pathway, is inactive. Vitamin C must therefore come from the diet, mainly fresh fruit and vegetables, and it is easily destroyed by heat and storage. Body stores last only weeks to a few months, so scurvy appears soon after intake stops.

In the rough endoplasmic reticulum, newly made pro-alpha chains are modified before they fold. Prolyl 4-hydroxylase converts proline in the Y position of the Gly-X-Y repeat to 4-hydroxyproline, prolyl 3-hydroxylase makes a smaller amount of 3-hydroxyproline, and lysyl hydroxylase converts lysine to hydroxylysine. These enzymes use Fe2+, O2, and alpha-ketoglutarate. Their iron is sometimes oxidized to Fe3+ during the reaction cycle, and ascorbate reduces it back to Fe2+. Without ascorbate the enzymes inactivate themselves and hydroxylation fails (MS-6).

Hydroxyproline stabilizes the triple helix by fixing the proline ring in the shape the helix requires and by adding water-mediated hydrogen bonds. Underhydroxylated chains form helices that melt below body temperature, 37 °C (98.6 °F), so they cannot fold stably. Most are retained in the endoplasmic reticulum and degraded, and secretion of collagen falls. Lack of hydroxylysine reduces glycosylation and the hydroxylysine-derived cross-links formed by lysyl oxidase, so the collagen that is secreted makes weak fibrils.

blocks.title: From ascorbate deficiency to fragile tissue
steps: Ascorbate is absent
Hydroxylase iron stays oxidized; enzymes inactivate
Proline and lysine are underhydroxylated
Triple helix is unstable at body temperature
Chains are degraded; less collagen is secreted
Fewer hydroxylysine cross-links weaken fibrils
Fragile vessels, poor healing, thin osteoid
blocks.caption: The defect is quantitative and qualitative: less collagen reaches the matrix, and what reaches it is weak.

blocks.text: The tissues that fail first are those that depend on continuous collagen synthesis. Capillaries rely on type IV collagen in their basement membrane and on supporting perivascular connective tissue, both of which need hydroxylated collagen, so they rupture under ordinary pressure and bleeding appears in skin, gums, muscle, and joints. Wound healing depends on new type III and then type I collagen; wounds gain little tensile strength, and old scars, whose collagen is remodeled continuously, can break down. In bone, osteoblasts produce too little osteoid, which is the reverse of rickets: there the osteoid is plentiful but unmineralized, while in scurvy mineral is available but there is little matrix to receive it.

Ascorbate also serves dopamine beta-hydroxylase and two enzymes of carnitine synthesis, which helps explain early fatigue, and it reduces dietary Fe3+ to Fe2+ for absorption, which links scurvy to iron deficiency.

sections.title: Scurvy: findings, risk groups, and how it differs from a bleeding disorder

blocks.text: Scurvy begins with nonspecific fatigue, malaise, irritability, and aching limbs after about one to three months of very low intake. Specific signs follow as collagen-dependent tissues fail, and nearly every one can be traced to fragile vessels or weak connective tissue.

blocks.title: Scurvy findings and their mechanisms
rows: Red to purple spots around hair follicles, mainly on the legs
Fragile capillaries rupture where hydrostatic pressure is highest
Coiled, fragmented hairs with follicular hyperkeratosis
Abnormal hair keratinization, thought to involve defective disulfide bonding
Swollen, spongy, purple gums that bleed; loose teeth
Fragile gingival vessels and weak periodontal collagen; spared where no teeth are present
Wounds fail to close; old scars may reopen
Capillary rupture under ordinary mechanical stress
Severe limb pain, refusal to move the legs
Bleeding lifts the loosely attached periosteum from bone
Blood loss, poor nonheme iron absorption, often coexisting folate deficiency
blocks.caption: Skin, gums, and joints bleed because their vessels lack collagen support, not because clotting fails.

blocks.text: In a child, scurvy presents with painful legs. The infant lies still with the hips and knees flexed and cries when the legs are handled, a picture called pseudoparalysis. Subperiosteal hemorrhage is painful because it strips the periosteum. Fractures through the weak metaphysis and a scorbutic rosary at the costochondral junctions may also occur; unlike the smooth rachitic rosary, the scorbutic rosary is angular, because the sternum sinks back behind the rib ends, and often tender. Radiographs show thin cortices and a dense line of calcified cartilage at the metaphysis with a lucent band of poor bone beneath it, where fractures occur.

Risk follows diet. Adults at risk eat few fruits and vegetables: older adults living alone on a limited diet, people with alcohol use disorder, people with food insecurity or very restrictive eating (including children with autism and selective eating), and people with malabsorption or on dialysis, which removes water-soluble vitamins. Smoking raises the requirement through oxidative turnover. Infant scurvy, usually after about 6 months of age, occurs when formula or breast milk is replaced by heat-treated cow milk or other foods without vitamin C.

Diagnosis rests on the clinical picture and a low plasma ascorbate, below about 0.2 mg/dL (11 micromol/L). Platelet count, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time are normal. That combination, mucocutaneous and deep bleeding with normal coagulation tests, separates scurvy from thrombocytopenia, vitamin K deficiency, and hemophilia, each of which can also cause hemarthrosis.

blocks.title: Painful legs in a 14-month-old
blocks.text: A toddler fed mainly boiled cow milk and crackers will not stand, screams when the legs are moved, and has swollen, bleeding gums around erupted teeth. Platelets, PT, and PTT are normal. Rickets is unlikely to explain this picture: it causes bowing and wide wrists but not acute pain on handling, gum bleeding, or subperiosteal hemorrhage. A coagulation defect is excluded by the normal tests. The diet lacks vitamin C, boiling destroys what little milk contains, and fragile vessels bleed beneath the periosteum and in the gums, so scurvy fits every finding.

blocks.predict: A man with alcohol use disorder has a hemarthrosis, perifollicular hemorrhages, and normal PT, PTT, and platelets. Why are the tests normal if he bleeds so easily?
blocks.explain: Those tests measure platelets and clotting factors, which are intact. The defect is in the vessel wall and its supporting collagen, which ruptures under ordinary stress; clotting at the site works normally once bleeding starts.
blocks.check: The mechanism table and the diagnosis paragraph.

integration.text: These three disorders show the two separate requirements for strong bone: a sound collagen matrix and mineral deposited within it. Scurvy fails the first: hydroxylation, a biochemical step inside the endoplasmic reticulum, is lost, so matrix is scarce and weak while mineral supply is normal. Rickets and osteomalacia fail the second: the matrix is normal or abundant, but the calcium phosphate product, set by the gut, kidney, liver, skin, and the PTH and FGF23 loops, is too low. Osteoporosis differs from both, being too little bone of normal composition, which is why its laboratory panel is normal. Pathology, anatomy, and biochemistry meet at the growth plate, where rickets and scurvy produce opposite metaphyseal changes.

The limits matter for exam reasoning. Serum calcium is defended by PTH and is a late and insensitive marker, so phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, PTH, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D carry the diagnosis. Thresholds for vitamin D sufficiency differ between expert bodies, and children have higher normal alkaline phosphatase and phosphate than adults, so values must be read against age-specific ranges. Scurvy is uncommon in high-income settings but persists in predictable risk groups, and its bleeding with normal coagulation tests is the distinction most often tested.

summary: Mineralization needs an adequate calcium phosphate product and alkaline phosphatase to clear pyrophosphate; osteoblasts keep making osteoid when mineral is lacking.
In vitamin D deficiency, secondary hyperparathyroidism holds calcium near normal but causes phosphaturia, so low phosphate is what usually stops mineralization.
The same defect causes rickets when growth plates are open and osteomalacia after they close.
Risk factors act at skin synthesis, intake and absorption, hepatic or renal hydroxylation, or catabolism; inducing anticonvulsants speed inactivation of vitamin D metabolites.
Osteomalacia: diffuse bone pain, proximal weakness, Looser zones, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase and PTH, low 25-hydroxyvitamin D, calcium low or normal.
Rickets: craniotabes, frontal bossing, rachitic rosary, wide wrists, bowed legs, and widened, cupped, frayed metaphyses.
X-linked hypophosphatemia: PHEX loss raises FGF23, causing phosphaturia and low calcitriol with normal calcium and normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
Vitamin C keeps prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase iron reduced; without it collagen helices are unstable, less collagen is secreted, and cross-linking is weak.
Scurvy: perifollicular hemorrhage, corkscrew hairs, bleeding gums, poor healing, hemarthrosis, and subperiosteal hemorrhage in children, with normal platelets, PT, and PTT.
Rickets has plentiful unmineralized osteoid; scurvy has too little osteoid with normal mineral supply.

verify: Vitamin D status thresholds differ: about 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) as sufficient (Institute of Medicine), 30 ng/mL in older Endocrine Society guidance, and deficiency below 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) in the global consensus on nutritional rickets. Confirm the cutoff NABNE uses.
Adult reference ranges for calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and PTH vary by laboratory; children have higher normal phosphate and alkaline phosphatase. Values here are approximate.

The mechanisms of bone pain (periosteal stretch by hydrated osteoid) and of corkscrew hairs (defective keratin disulfide bonding) are commonly cited but not firmly established; they are stated as probable.
The time to clinical scurvy (about 1 to 3 months of near-zero intake) and the plasma ascorbate cutoff (about 0.2 mg/dL, 11 micromol/L) vary slightly between sources.

Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms and radiographic terms Milkman fracture (for Looser zones), Harrison sulcus, and the scurvy signs Frankel line, Trummerfeld zone, Wimberger ring, and Pelkan spur, which this chapter describes without naming most of them.
The age range given for craniotabes (usually under about 6 months) and for physiologic genu varum (until about 18 to 24 months) are approximate and differ slightly between pediatric sources.
